notes:
Here is a verse-by-verse commentary on Deuteronomy 30, drawing from the sources accessed across multiple theological traditions.

---

## DEUTERONOMY 30 — VERSE-BY-VERSE NOTES

### Overview

Deuteronomy 30 falls within Moses' third major address (Deut 29:2–30:20), which follows the covenant-treaty pattern of the ancient Near East and functions as a covenant-renewal ceremony. After detailing the blessings and curses (chapters 27–28), Moses now looks beyond the coming judgment to a future restoration. The chapter contains two major sections: (1) promises of restoration after repentance (vv. 1–10), and (2) a concluding charge to choose life (vv. 11–20).

---

### v. 1 — "When all these things come upon you—the blessings and curses I have set before you—and you call them to mind in all the nations to which the LORD your God has banished you…"

**Traditional Reading:** Moses here speaks not of a mere possibility but of a certainty. The Hebrew begins with "when" (not "if"), indicating that Israel *will* experience both the blessings and curses, and *will* be exiled among the nations. The phrase "call them to mind" literally means "bring back to your heart" (Hebrew *shub*). It describes a future moment when exiled Israel will remember God's words and recognise their circumstances as the consequence of covenant disobedience.

- **Ellicott** notes that "the curse is still upon them, and therefore this chapter contemplates the possibility of a restoration still to come." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/30.htm)
- **Precept Austin** stresses the "WHEN, not IF" nature, calling it a prophecy that "Israel will indeed break her covenant with Yahweh." It ties this to the Great Tribulation and "the time of Jacob's trouble" (Jer 30:7), arguing for a yet-future final fulfillment. (preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-30-commentary)
- **Constable** views this as the first of seven steps in Israel's prophetic history: dispersion for disobedience. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-30.html)
- **David Guzik (Enduring Word):** "From the height of blessing during the reigns of David and Solomon, to the depth of cursing at the fall of Jerusalem, Israel's history has been a legacy of either being blessed or cursed under the terms of the old covenant." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/)

---

### v. 2 — "…and when you and your children return to the LORD your God and obey His voice with all your heart and all your soul according to everything I am giving you today…"

**Traditional Reading:** The condition for restoration is genuine, wholehearted repentance — a "return" (*shub*) to Yahweh involving both inward heart-devotion and outward obedience. It is a national repentance, involving "you and your children," not merely a generation but the covenant people as a whole.

- **Guzik:** "As Israel would return to the LORD, God would bless them and bring them back from captivity, having compassion on them." He quotes Trapp: "By sin we run away from God; by repentance we return to him." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/)
- **The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics)** emphasises that "in man's conversion, it is the sinner, not God, who changes… Israel is saved at last, not by any lowering of the standard of holiness… but by Israel coming round to God's way of thinking." (biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/30.htm)
- **John Piper (Reformed Baptist):** Notes the tension — God demands wholehearted return, yet Deuteronomy 29:4 said God had "not given you a heart to understand." The answer to this dilemma comes in verse 6. (desiringgod.org/messages/an-impossible-covenant)

---

### v. 3 — "…then He will restore you from captivity and have compassion on you and gather you from all the nations to which the LORD your God has scattered you."

**Traditional Reading:** God promises to "turn" Israel's captivity. The Hebrew verb here is intriguing — it is not in the active voice but a form that rabbinic tradition understood to mean that the Shechinah (divine presence) itself shares in Israel's exile and will "return" with them. The gathering is from "all the nations," suggesting a worldwide regathering beyond just Babylon.

- **Ellicott** explains the rabbinic observation: "in some way the Shechinah is abiding upon Israel during the stress of their captivity, and whensoever they are redeemed, He has prescribed Redemption for Himself, that He will return with them." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/30.htm)
- **Guzik:** This was fulfilled *in part* by the return from Babylon under Ezra and Nehemiah, but "the ultimate fulfillment of this would await the Twentieth Century, when God would regather Israel in the Promised Land." He argues the modern regathering is "larger, broader, more sovereign, and more miraculous" than the Babylonian return. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/)
- **Precept Austin** disagrees with partial-fulfillment views, insisting that after Babylon "Israel still did not obey Him with a whole heart. And so this prophecy awaits a final fulfillment that is yet future." (preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-30-commentary)

---

### v. 4 — "Even if you have been banished to the farthest horizon, He will gather you and return you from there."

**Traditional Reading:** No distance of exile is beyond God's ability to regather His people. The LXX rendering of "the farthest horizon" (literally "the outmost parts of heaven") is traceable in Jesus' words in Matthew 24:31 about the gathering of the elect "from the one end of heaven to the other."

- **Ellicott** notes the LXX connection to Matthew 24:31. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/30.htm)
- **Adam Clarke (1811),** cited by Guzik, recognised that since this scattering is "among all nations," it cannot refer merely to the Babylonian captivity but must point to a future, global regathering. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/)
- **Gill** sees this as a prophecy of the latter-day conversion of the Jews and their return "to their own land." (mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/30.htm, from search excerpt)

---

### v. 5 — "And the LORD your God will bring you into the land your fathers possessed, and you will take possession of it. He will cause you to prosper and multiply more than your fathers."

**Traditional Reading:** The restoration is specifically to *the land* — the land "your fathers possessed," i.e., Canaan/Palestine. The promise includes not just return but prosperity and numerical increase beyond the patriarchal era.

- **Guzik** notes that the British offer of Uganda for a Jewish homeland would *not* have fulfilled this prophecy: "This could only be fulfilled in the land which your fathers possessed." He sees modern Israel's prosperity and population as a partial fulfillment. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/)
- **Constable** notes: "While the repossession of the land can be said to some extent to have been fulfilled by the return of the Jews following the Babylonian exile… the greater prosperity and population was not achieved in Old Testament times. In fact, it still awaits realization in any literal sense." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-30.html)
- **Ellicott:** "It is very difficult to interpret these words of any land except Palestine." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/30.htm)

---

### v. 6 — "The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts and the hearts of your descendants, and you will love Him with all your heart and with all your soul, so that you may live."

**Traditional Reading:** This is the theological high point of the chapter and arguably of Deuteronomy. Where Deuteronomy 10:16 commanded Israel to "circumcise your hearts," here God promises that *He Himself* will do it. This is a unilateral, sovereign work of inward transformation — what Christian theology calls regeneration. The phrase "circumcision of the heart" appears only here, Deuteronomy 10:16, and Jeremiah 4:4 in the OT.

- **Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** Views this as the "spiritual dimension of the restoration" that "has not yet been accomplished." Modern Israel is largely secular; the spiritual circumcision awaits Israel's turning to Jesus as Messiah. He links it to Ezekiel 36:26–27 and Romans 11:26. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/)
- **John Piper (Reformed Baptist):** Calls this "the most precious, most hope-filled verse in the entire book." He argues it answers the dilemma of Deuteronomy 29:4 (God had not given them a heart to understand): "God unilaterally, sovereignly cuts this God-spurning deadness away! And thus 'cuts' a new covenant." This is God "sovereignly securing — guaranteeing, bringing about — the purpose of creation." (desiringgod.org/messages/an-impossible-covenant)
- **Constable (Dispensational):** "Here Moses anticipated a new covenant that eventually replaced the old Mosaic Covenant… Just as circumcision of the flesh symbolized outward identification… so circumcision of the heart… speaks of internal identification with him in what might be called regeneration in Christian theology." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-30.html)
- **Precept Austin** calls this "the key verse in this section" and notes it is "synonymous with their entry into the New Covenant." (preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-30-commentary)
- **Gill (Baptist, 18th Century):** "There is no love to God in the heart before this inward and spiritual circumcision of it: it is a fruit of the Spirit in conversion when the affections are taken off of other things, and set on Christ." (mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/30.htm, from search excerpt)
- **The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics):** "Repentance leads to entire renewal of a man's nature… The repentant Jew discovered that the circumcision of the flesh effected nothing to deter from sin; now he perceives that circumcision of heart is the only real safeguard." (biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/30.htm)

**Tradition Differences on v. 6:**

- **Reformed Covenant Theology** (e.g., Westminster Confession) sees this as a promise of the covenant of grace, administered differently in the Old and New Testaments but substantially the same. The "circumcision of the heart" is regeneration, the same reality signified by baptism in the new covenant era. (monergism.com, from search excerpt)
- **Reformed Baptist / New Covenant Theology** (e.g., Piper, also reflected at TGC) agrees this is regeneration but insists the new covenant community is entirely regenerate (contra paedobaptism). "The trajectory of the New Covenant points to a wholly regenerate covenant community." (thegospelcoalition.org, from search excerpt)
- **Dispensationalism** (e.g., Constable, Ryrie) sees this as a promise specifically to *ethnic Israel* to be fulfilled at Christ's second coming and in the millennium — distinct from the church. "God has a future for Israel as a nation that is distinct from the future of the church." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-30.html)

---

### v. 7 — "Then the LORD your God will put all these curses upon your enemies who hate you and persecute you."

**Traditional Reading:** When Israel is restored, God will reverse the curses — transferring them from Israel onto her enemies. This echoes the Abrahamic promise: "I will bless those who bless you, and whoever curses you I will curse" (Gen 12:3).

- **Guzik:** These promises "show how foolish it was for Christians and the institutional church to persecute the Jewish people." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/)
- **Constable** lists this as step six in the prophetic sequence: "the judgment of Israel's oppressors." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-30.html)
- **Precept Austin / Hannah's Outline:** "The promise of judgment on Israel's enemies." (preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-30-commentary)

---

### vv. 8–10 — "And you will again obey the voice of the LORD… the LORD will again delight in your goodness… if you obey… and turn to Him with all your heart and with all your soul."

**Traditional Reading:** The restoration produces genuine, sustained obedience, not the cyclical rebellion of Israel's past. God will "again rejoice over you for good" — a striking image of divine delight. The "if" in v. 10 (Hebrew *ki*, which can also mean "when" or "for") does not undercut the certainty of v. 6; rather, the obedience is the *result* of the heart-circumcision God performs.

- **Guzik:** "The Lord will again rejoice over the Jewish people, as He did over their fathers. All this will be seen when Israel turns to the LORD… as He is revealed in Jesus the Messiah." He sees ultimate fulfillment in the Millennium. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/)
- **Piper:** Emphasises that God's delight in prospering His people is tied to their having become morally beautiful through heart-transformation. "Surely that does not mean that He delights in doing good to you while finding you yourself to be morally ugly and displeasing." This is about the "beautification of the people of God." (desiringgod.org/messages/an-impossible-covenant)
- **Ellicott** notes the LXX translates the Hebrew *ki* as "if," but the Hebrew means "for" or "when." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/30.htm)

---

### v. 11 — "For this commandment I give you today is not too difficult for you or beyond your reach."

**Traditional Reading:** "This commandment" (*mitzvah*) refers to the covenant obligation as a whole — the duty of loving and obeying God. The Hebrew phrase translated "not too difficult" (*lo niphleit*) literally means "not too wonderful" or "not beyond comprehension." The point is accessibility and clarity, not ease of performance by unaided human effort.

- **Constable:** "The point at issue here was not the ease or even possibility of keeping the word of the Lord… but of even knowing what it was. Contrary to the inscrutable and enigmatic ways of the pagan gods, the Lord's purposes and will for his people are crystal clear." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-30.html)
- **Guzik:** "Israel could indeed keep this covenant. God did not expect the impossible from Israel when He expected them to keep this covenant." However, he clarifies that the old covenant included sacrifice and choice, not just law; God never expected perfect law-obedience to save. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/)
- **Piper** ties vv. 11–14 directly to v. 6: only because God circumcises the heart and puts His word in the mouth and heart can the commandment be "not too hard." Without that, "with man it is impossible (Deuteronomy 29:4), because we are spiritually dead and blind." (desiringgod.org/messages/an-impossible-covenant)
- **Ellicott** titles this section (vv. 11–14) "The Law of the Righteousness Which Is of Faith." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/30.htm)

---

### vv. 12–13 — "It is not in heaven… And it is not beyond the sea…"

**Traditional Reading:** Moses uses rhetorical questions to emphasise that God's revealed will is not inaccessible. No heroic quest to heaven or dangerous sea-voyage is needed to discover it — God has already spoken plainly.

- **Ellicott** notes that St. Paul in Romans 10:6–7 adapts these very words: "'Who shall ascend into heaven?' (that is, to bring Christ down from above)… 'Who shall descend into the deep?' (that is, to bring up Christ again from the dead)." Paul substitutes "the deep" (*abyss*) for "beyond the sea," interpreting the passage Christologically. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/30.htm)
- **Guzik** adds: "Paul used this passage in Romans 10 to show that under the old covenant, Israelites could grasp salvation through the sacrificial system pointing to Christ, just as we now see it in bright sunlight." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/)

---

### v. 14 — "But the word is very near you; it is in your mouth and in your heart, so that you may obey it."

**Traditional Reading:** God's word is not external or remote but internalised. This verse is famously quoted by Paul in Romans 10:8 as "the word of faith which we preach" — identifying the "word" with the gospel of Christ.

- **Ellicott** contrasts the Jewish and Christian readings: The Jewish commentator Rashi says, "The Law is given you in Scripture and in tradition" (written and oral). But Paul says: "The word is nigh thee, in thy mouth, and in thine heart, that is, the word of faith which we preach; that if thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus, and shalt believe in thine heart that God hath raised Him from the dead, thou shalt be saved." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/30.htm)
- **Guzik:** "What the Israelite could see, they could see as if it was by moonlight. Since the incarnation, life, ministry, suffering, death, resurrection, and ascension of Jesus, all this is seen by the brightest sunlight." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/)
- **Piper:** "When God puts his word not on tablets of stone, or pages of parchment, but in your mouth and in your heart, you not only can love God; you will." (desiringgod.org/messages/an-impossible-covenant)

---

### vv. 15–16 — "See, I have set before you today life and goodness, as well as death and disaster. For I am commanding you today to love the LORD your God…"

**Traditional Reading:** Moses presents the classic "two ways" — life/good versus death/evil (or disaster). This is not merely about physical life in the land but encompasses the whole covenant relationship. The choice is embodied in concrete actions: loving God, walking in His ways, keeping His commandments.

- **Guzik:** "Under the terms of the Old Covenant, Israel had a choice: life or death, good or evil. It was up to them." He notes this was "an appeal to all Israel but spoken to them as individuals." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/)
- **Constable** observes that "the notion of choice, with its implication of freedom to determine one's own actions or mode of life, is one which is characteristic of Deuteronomy. God chooses, but human beings also have that freedom." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-30.html)
- **Precept Austin** notes the "two ways" motif is "analogous to the TWO WAYS in the great opening Psalm 1," and also Jesus' two ways in Matthew 7:13–14. (preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-30-commentary)

---

### vv. 17–18 — "But if your heart turns away… I declare to you today that you will surely perish; you shall not prolong your days in the land…"

**Traditional Reading:** The warning is stark: apostasy — turning to other gods — brings certain destruction and loss of the land. The language is covenantal curse language.

- **Guzik:** "If this Old Covenant is inferior to the New Covenant, and if there was a high price to pay for rejecting the Old Covenant, should we not know there is an even greater penalty for rejecting an even greater covenant? (Hebrews 10:28–29)." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/)

---

### v. 19 — "I call heaven and earth as witnesses against you today that I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing. Therefore choose life, so that you and your descendants may live…"

**Traditional Reading:** Moses invokes creation itself — heaven and earth — as permanent, enduring witnesses to the covenant choice. This reflects ancient Near Eastern treaty practice, but with a monotheistic adaptation: instead of calling upon pagan gods as witnesses, Israel's covenant calls upon creation.

- **Guzik** quotes Merrill: "In similar ancient Near Eastern legal transactions the witnesses usually were the gods of the respective litigants, but the monotheism of Israel's faith dictated that such appeal be to creation, to heaven and earth, for only it would endure into future ages." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/)
- **Constable:** "Moses called the permanent, unchanging heaven and earth to witness the making of this covenant." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-30.html)
- **The Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics)** on "choose life": "Moses' plea to 'choose life' reveals God's heart — though Israel had genuine freedom to choose, God clearly preferred they choose obedience and blessing." (biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/30.htm)
- **Guzik** adds: "Man today is confronted with the choice. But since the life, death, and resurrection of Jesus, the choice focuses first not on 'Will I obey God or not?' but on 'Will I trust in Jesus for my standing before God?'" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/)

---

### v. 20 — "…and that you may love the LORD your God, obey Him, and hold fast to Him. For He is your life, and He will prolong your life in the land that the LORD swore to give to your fathers, to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob."

**Traditional Reading:** Choosing life is defined in relational terms: loving God, obeying His voice, and "holding fast" (*dabaq* — cleaving, clinging) to Him. The verse climaxes with the declaration that God Himself *is* your life — not merely the giver of life. The chapter ends by anchoring the promise in the patriarchal covenant (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob).

- **Ellicott:** "This is the Old Testament form of a well-known saying in the New Testament… 'I am the resurrection and the life. He that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live' (John 11:25–26)." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/30.htm)
- **Guzik:** "To love God this way… means to obey His voice… to cling to Him… to regard Him as our life and length of days, because if we love and trust Him, He is not part of our life, He is our life." He quotes Adam Clarke: "Without love there can be no obedience… Without obedience love is fruitless and dead." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/)
- **Constable:** "The highest motive, love for God, would enable the Israelites to obey the Lord steadfastly." (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-30.html)
- **Gill** sees the land promise as "typical of eternal life and happiness; which is had, not through man's obedience to the law, but through the obedience and righteousness of Christ." (mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/deuteronomy/30.htm, from search excerpt)
- **Piper** closes his sermon on this passage by applying it directly: "Choose life, that you and your offspring may live, loving the Lord your God, obeying his voice and holding fast to him, for he is your life." (desiringgod.org/messages/an-impossible-covenant)

---

## TRADITION DISTINCTIVES — KEY DIFFERENCES

### The Future of Israel: Dispensational vs. Covenant/Reformed vs. Non-Dispensational Readings

This is the main tradition divide on Deuteronomy 30.

- **Dispensational (e.g., Constable, Precept Austin, older Guzik):** Reads vv. 1–10 as a distinct "Palestinian Covenant" promising ethnic Israel a literal future: physical regathering to the land, national conversion, millennial prosperity. The modern state of Israel is a partial, providential fulfillment; full fulfillment awaits the second coming. The church does not replace or absorb these promises. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/deuteronomy-30.html; preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-30-commentary)

- **Reformed Covenant Theology (e.g., Westminster Confession, Monergism):** Sees one covenant of grace administered differently across redemptive history. Old and New Testament believers form one people of God. The promises of land and restoration find their fulfillment in Christ and the church — either spiritually (the land as type of inheritance in Christ) or in the new heavens and new earth. Circumcision and baptism signify the same spiritual reality. (monergism.com, from search excerpt)

- **Reformed Baptist / New Covenant Theology (e.g., Piper, also at TGC):** Agrees with covenant theology that there is one people of God, but insists the new covenant community is *regenerate only* (no mixed community of believers and unbelievers). Deuteronomy 30:6 promises regeneration; it is fulfilled in the new covenant through faith in Christ. Unlike dispensationalism, does not expect a distinct future for ethnic Israel separate from the church. Unlike paedobaptist covenant theology, insists baptism is for professing believers only. (desiringgod.org; thegospelcoalition.org, from search excerpts)

### Paul's Use of Deuteronomy 30:11–14 in Romans 10

- **Lutheran / Reformation reading:** Paul's use of Deuteronomy 30:11–14 in Romans 10:6–8 is a classic “law-gospel” hermeneutic. Moses' words about the law being “near you” are reinterpreted by Paul to refer to “the word of faith” — Christ Himself. The law drives us to Christ, who alone makes the word truly near. (ellicott contrasts the Jewish reading with Paul's; biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/30.htm)
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** Emphasises that Paul shows salvation was always by grace through faith, even under the old covenant, via the sacrificial system pointing to Christ. The difference between old and new is not the *means* of salvation but the *clarity*. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/)

### The “Choose Life” Call: Sovereignty and Human Responsibility

- **Reformed (Piper):** The call to “choose life” is genuine and urgent, but it can only be obeyed because of the prior work of God circumcising the heart (v. 6). The command does not imply unaided human ability; it is effective through God's regenerating grace. (desiringgod.org/messages/an-impossible-covenant)
- **Wesleyan/Arminian-leaning:** The choice is genuinely free. The Pulpit Commentary stresses: "Man is accountable for his actions, because they are his; were he necessitated by fate, or sovereign constraint, they could not be his" (Clarke, cited by Guzik). The choice is real because God has enabled it, but it remains a human decision. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/deuteronomy-30/; biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/deuteronomy/30.htm)

### Prosperity Teaching Note

None of the sources accessed promote a "prosperity gospel" reading of vv. 9–10 (where God makes Israel "abound"). The traditional reading consistently ties the prosperity promises to covenant obedience under the old covenant specifically for Israel, or views them typologically as pointing to spiritual blessing in Christ. Guzik explicitly ties ultimate fulfillment to the Millennium, not to a present-day claim on material wealth. No Word of Faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter was found in the designated sources.

---

## OTHER VIEWS

### NetBible.org / Modern Scholarship

The NET Bible notes (cited at Precept Austin) translate v. 1: "When you have experienced all these things, both the blessings and the curses I have set before you, you will reflect upon them in all the nations where the LORD your God has banished you." Modern scholarship tends to see this chapter as a late-exilic or post-exilic composition, though traditional commentators uniformly treat it as Mosaic prophecy. No Bible Odyssey or NET Bible pages were directly accessible within the search limits, but Precept Austin extensively uses NET Bible notes throughout its commentary. (preceptaustin.org/deuteronomy-30-commentary)

### Catholic and Orthodox Readings

No pages from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org were returned in the searches. The available material does not include specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary on this chapter.

### Older Jewish Reading (from Ellicott's citation of Rashi)

Rashi (medieval Jewish commentator) interprets v. 14 as referring to the Law given in written Scripture *and* oral tradition. This contrasts sharply with Paul's Christological reading in Romans 10. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/deuteronomy/30.htm)
